title: Another one writes the code
abstract: Generative AI can now write code across the data science lifecycle and produce plausible interpretations, challenging core assumptions about what beginners should learn and how they should be assessed. This talk examines the redesign of an introductory data science course at Duke University in response to these shifts. Some changes were made because of AI, including new in-class assessments; others were made thanks to AI, such as integrating just-in-time feedback in the IDE. I will discuss what changed, what failed, what improved, and how student feedback—ranging from enthusiasm to skepticism—is shaping an evolving approach to teaching data science in the age of generative AI.

title: What context do your AI agents actually need?
abstract:
Context window! AGENTS.md! Custom instructions! Agent skills! Max tokens??

If you use AI agents in your data science work, you've probably heard tips about these things and already use some of them. But does it actually feel like your agents have the context they need about your data, packages, and analysis? Or do you find yourself re-explaining your data, spending more time editing agent output than doing the actual task, or using up tokens faster than you'd like?

Drawing on experience building Positron's agent features, this talk covers how to manage context: what kinds matter (from data to project structure), how to include them (files you write in advance vs. fetching info on the fly), and how to get results you don't have to rewrite.

title: AI Agents Deserve R
abstract: R users have deep domain knowledge and finely-tuned workflows. You should not have to abandon them to use AI. The R ecosystem already has incredible building blocks: ellmer, shinychat, ragnar, and more. This talk will cover some new entrants that such as deputy, dsprrr, and shinymcp that grow the stack. Built on ellmer, deputy adds agentic workflows. This includes agents that plan, use tools, and solve multi-step tasks. dsprrr lets you program, not prompt, your LLM pipelines. Compose modules and let data-driven optimization tune for you. With coding agents making it easier than ever to port innovations across languages, R's AI story has never been stronger. Stay in an ecosystem you love and bring agents with you.

title: Demography in the Age of Policy Uncertainty
abstract:
This talk showcases a dashboard that creates demographic projections for regions across the United State of America to help drive impactful policies aimed at creating better human outcomes. The tool leverages the power of spatial statistics in R, Shiny, and the Apache Arrow ecosystem to efficiently provide regionally specific insights.

Forecasts and projections are always challenging, however federal policy uncertainty and an ongoing erosion to data quality are impeding our ability to plan for the future. This talk discusses the headwinds to demographic data creation and dissemination at the federal level and the implications this could have for local jurisdictions to provide key services to their communities.

title: MCP, or not MCP
abstract: Model Context Protocol is a standard for defining tools that can be made available to LLMs and AI applications. There’s a lot of noise out there about what you should use to get the best results from AI, so in this talk, I will provide some guidance on when you should use MCP, and when you should reach for some other tool. I will describe cases where MCP is the right tool for the job, and when other things, like skills or other context files, are better. I will also devote attention to questions of security and authentication, which are important for MCP. Some critics of MCP have argued that they are risky, and I’ll discuss why. Then, I will show how you can use MCP in a way that actually improves your security and will delight IT admins.

title: Outgrowing Spreadsheets: Rebuilding Research Data Collection with Shiny and Posit Connect
abstract: I’ll share how our nonprofit research team transformed a fragile, spreadsheet-based data collection process into a sustainable system using Shiny and Posit Connect. We publish a data set on 2,500 hospital financial assistance programs and how they collect medical debt from patients. Our team collected this data using Google Forms and sheets. It technically worked, but it was fragile, slow, and completely dependent on one person (me). When we finally got Posit Connect, we rebuilt the system based on three principles: structured data entry, automated validation, and recorded updates. This talk shares the before-and-after architecture and practical lessons for teams ready to outgrow spreadsheets and design sustainable workflows.

title: The Unreasonable Effectiveness of Quarto
abstract: Quarto markets itself as a publishing framework. But at its core, Quarto is an abstraction layer separating *content* from *format* — a distinction that turns out to be remarkably powerful in the era of AI agents. When an LLM generates a document, content and structure emerge together in a single probabilistic pass, but nothing in that output is guaranteed. Quarto's code-at-render-time model solves this by letting the LLM build the structure while allowing the content that must be exact to be rendered deterministically from data files. The result is reproducible and auditable output that stays correct as your content changes, without needing to re-prompt models. This talk brings the agent + Quarto workflow to life with concrete examples, from a simple one-page PDF to a fully interactive multi-page dashboard integrating JavaScript libraries, Shinylive, and React, showing how asking an LLM for a qmd file instead of a finished document dramatically reduces token overhead while producing more dynamic, trustworthy, and maintainable output.

title: Say Yes to the Request - From Helping One to Empowering Many
abstract: R adoption surged when we embraced one rule: say yes to every question and turn each insight into something that lasts. To hit GSK’s 50% R-by-2026 goal, STARburst—a small team of R experts—opened a helpdesk focused on high-touch support. Each interaction followed a deliberate user journey: we met people where they were, unblocked the immediate task, then used that same moment to teach reusable habits for open-source ways of working. In parallel, we logged every learning and gap, turning recurring issues into R and Quarto assets: daily blogs and FAQs first, then example libraries, hardened guidance, and improved R packages. Attendees will see how bite-sized, one-to-one help compounds into organization-wide R capability for the long haul.

title: SQL as a first-class language in your data science IDE
abstract: Data scientists spend a lot of time and effort writing SQL, yet most data science environments treat it as an afterthought or a separate workflow, forcing you to switch tools, copy results between windows, and lose context along the way. In this talk, learn how Positron brings SQL into the same environment where you write Python and R code. We’ll walk through connecting to databases, writing queries with intelligent code completion, executing SQL in a dedicated console, and exploring results in the Data Explorer. You’ll see how keeping SQL alongside your other data science work reduces friction and errors. This talk is for data scientists and analysts who regularly query databases and want to stop context-switching between tools.
track_title: The Modern Data Science Stack... still SQL

title: A Grammar of Graphics for SQL
abstract: SQL has been with us for many years, but despite its age it is still a cornerstone of data-analysis everywhere. The quick success of DuckDB shows this more than ever. However,  SQL is often used as the first step to extract data, delegating any search for insight to a different programming language or environment. I would like to present ggsql, an extension of SQL that provides a grammar of graphics on top of SQL and allows you to create visualisations directly within your query. ggsql is a modular tool, build to interface directly with your data source and optimised for use by an LLM based data analysis workflow due to its lack of runtime.
track_title: The Modern Data Science Stack... still SQL

title: One Report, Many Audiences: Role‑Based Views in Posit Connect
abstract: Harvard University’s decentralized structure creates diverse data needs across its many schools. Our central institutional research office uses Posit Connect to share data and reports, but not every person should see the same content. To address this, we published a Shiny app on Posit Connect that detects the logged‑in user and dynamically tailors what they see. This means that a single report can securely serve many audiences. This talk will walk through how the pieces fit together and offer a model for organizations seeking scalable, user‑aware reporting.

title: Quarto Wiki Chatbot
abstract: After a year of compiling onboarding, technical, and other documentation into a centralized Quarto Wiki, NASA’s People Analytics team still struggled to quickly search for needed information. We developed an integrated chatbot, which surfaces and cites relevant content to answer user questions - processing QMD files into a vector database, developing a Python RAG pipeline, and embedding an R Shiny chat window into the Quarto site’s interface. To reduce latency and long-term LLM costs, DuckDB caches and scores prior query-response pairs for selective reuse. The system can be deployed on Posit Connect or run locally, illustrating a reproducible workflow for interactive, AI-assisted documentation. Presented by: Aliza Samad and Sofia Lendahl.

title: Scaling Reports: Template → Package → App
abstract: Farmers need to understand their soil data to guide management decisions, but advisors often lack time or coding expertise to generate interpretive reports that make the data actionable. To deliver multilingual, customizable soil health reports at scale, we 1) created a parameterized Quarto template, 2) expanded it into {soils}, an R package for technical users, and 3) developed Dirt Data Reports, a Shiny app for non-coders. From template to package to app, we’ll share lessons from building complementary tools that increase access to soil health insights and support real-world impact.

title: SQL Without Writing SQL: dbplyr for Serious Shiny Apps
abstract: You don't need to be an SQL expert or a DBA to build high-performance Shiny apps on large datasets. With dbplyr, you can write familiar dplyr code while it translates your pipelines into optimized SQL behind the scenes. In this talk we will explore how integrating Shiny with Postgres SQL and how the dplyr you write today can translate to better performing applications. We will cover practical patterns to keep computation in the database to create production-ready apps without leaving R.
track_title: The Modern Data Science Stack... still SQL

title: Keynote Session: How to Be Clear When You Can’t Be Certain
abstract: Sometimes, data visualization is about using charts to illustrate a key point or conclusion gleaned from analyzing the data. But what if you’re not sure what the conclusion is? Presenting examples from news reporting on the topics of elections, polling and economics, I will talk about how I have grappled with uncertainty and how to communicate it to the public.

title: For the community, by the community: The 10-year journey of R Weekly powered by open-source
abstract: For a decade, R Weekly has highlighted the innovations, creativity, and novel resources tailored to the R language across data science. Built and sustained by a small, volunteer curator team, the project demonstrates how open-source values—transparency, collaboration, and shared ownership—can power a lasting community initiative. This talk explores how R Weekly evolved, the workflows and infrastructure that keep it running, and the lessons learned from ten years of amplifying innovation. This talk will demonstrate how community-driven curation can strengthen ecosystems and inspire sustainable open-source contributions.

title: Interdependent Filters in Shiny Made Simple
abstract:
Developing interdependent filters in Shiny has always been tedious, requiring 
developers to rewrite custom ui and server logic for each new app. The new R 
package shinyfilters exists to eliminate this boilerplate. shinyfilters lets 
anyone create interdependent filters directly from data.frames. I am excited to 
show attendees how shinyfilters uses S7 to simplify interdependent filter logic, 
how to replace repetitive ui and server code with simple function calls, and 
how to extend shinyfilters for their own use cases.

title: Beyond Bootstrap: Building Custom Shiny UI Packages with AI
abstract:
Shiny developers have long been limited to Bootstrap and a handful of pre-built UI frameworks. But what if you could use Material UI, Ant Design, or any modern react.js web framework you love?

This talk demonstrates how AI can generate production-ready R packages that wrap your favorite UI frameworks for Shiny. We'll walk through using AI to translate JavaScript components into R bindings, handle dependencies, and create idiomatic interfaces—no JavaScript expertise required.

You'll see live examples, learn effective prompting patterns, and discover how to maintain AI-generated packages. Whether you want Material Design or Web Components, AI makes it possible to bring any UI framework into your Shiny apps.

title: Quarto Notebooks and Literate Programming in Positron
abstract: Quarto Notebooks, a new Positron feature, give you access to Jupyter's literate programming features without losing any of the benefits of working with plain text for editing, versioning, and collaborating. They are a natural evolution of the R Markdown Notebooks feature in RStudio into the modern, multi-lingual environment of Quarto and Positron. In this talk, I'll introduce this new way of working, and describe both its similarities and differences to its predecessor in RStudio. Finally, we'll spend some time comparing the different tools for literate programming in Positron, their tradeoffs, and how to choose the right one.

title: ADBC: A Faster Foundation for Database Connectivity in R, Python, and Beyond
abstract: dplyr was a revolution for R, and dbplyr was a smaller but important revolution for those of us who wanted to use databases without leaving behind the powerful and familiar syntax of dplyr. The arrow R package was another revolution of its own, letting us work with larger-than-memory data while still using dplyr syntax. Apache Arrow, the larger project of which the arrow R package is a part, also has a standard for database access: ADBC. In this talk, I’ll introduce ADBC, which works with R, Python, and other languages and is coming to dbplyr. I’ll give an intro to Arrow and ADBC, and show how to use a new command line tool, dbc, along with dbplyr, for fast, larger-than-memory database access that works seamlessly across R and Python.
track_title: The Modern Data Science Stack... still SQL

title: Yes And...AI in Your IDE
abstract: Large language models are now embedded in our IDEs, shaping how we code. Research suggests assistants don’t respond “neutrally”: how you ask and even cues about who is asking can shift what the model says. In this session, we’ll explore what that looks like with Posit’s AI tools that draw on IDE context. We’ll run simple “paired prompts”: same problem, different asker and ask-style, then compare their agreement, confidence, and whether the assistant challenges assumptions or amplifies them. This talk is about using LLMs as a learning partner: asking for explanations so the model helps you understand, not just produce. Bring curiosity, your critical thinking, and a healthy suspicion of anything that agrees with you a little too easily.
track_title: Being an informed and savvy AI user

title: Shiny design: Where humans and AI disagree
abstract: AI can generate Shiny dashboards, grade visual quality from screenshots, and tweak their own code. But do they actually like the same designs people do? We pitted automated visual scores against blind human rankings across dashboards built by different models, frameworks, and prompts. I'll share where machine taste matches human judgment, where it completely falls off, and what these gaps tell us about visual design. Finally, we'll look at how human input can spot the flaws in automated scoring so we can build far better AI evaluators.

title: From Tribal Knowledge to Trusted AI in Pharma
abstract:
Everyone wants to know how to build useful AI. We learned that the hardest part wasn’t the technical implementation at all.

We expected embeddings, entity extraction, retrieval pipelines, and plenty of AI plumbing. Instead, the work that mattered most was sitting with pharmaceutical sales reps, uncovering tribal knowledge, resolving conflicting definitions, and turning years of business logic from Shiny apps on Posit Connect into governed logic in Snowflake.

This talk shows what changed once we built around how people actually work. We’ll share how user feedback shaped the language, rules, UX, and priorities of the system, and how that human context made the AI more trustworthy, explainable, and useful in the field.
track_title: Being an informed and savvy AI user

title: Influence with Quarto: Designing Reports That Drive Decisions
abstract: Most people using Quarto already know how to render documents. This talk focuses on what comes next: elevating Quarto reports through design, layout, and narrative. Using a realistic example report, I’ll show how styling, visual hierarchy, and thoughtful structure can transform a technically correct analysis into a compelling story for decision-makers. The goal isn’t more code, but better communication: using the right data storytelling, CSS, and ggplot to create reports that feel intentional, polished, and impactful. Attendees will leave with concrete ideas to push their own Quarto reports beyond defaults.

title: Repotting and propagating my Shiny houseplant
abstract: My Shiny app started out as a single seed: one app.R. Its quick growth became restricted by its tiny pot as features tangled together. So, I repotted my app.R file into 11 modules to organize my UI and server logic. My Shiny plant kept growing, but with better structure. To share my thriving plant with friends and clients, I learned how to propagate cuttings to create new, similar apps by turning it into a package. This let me reuse the core code across apps, while making pieces customizable. To update calculations or aesthetics, I now update the package code once, rather than editing 10 different apps. This talk will walk through the app growth cycle, what triggers each step, and how to repot and propagate without killing your Shiny plant.

title: Hello, robot: Introducing humans to LLM’s
abstract: You know that AI can be transformative when used correctly, but how do you train your team – or organization – to be effective AI users? Last year we tackled this problem through a course that built foundational LLM skills for staff at Posit. By focusing on learner curiosity, personal experience and experimentation, we helped teams across the organization develop relevant skills with AI tools. In this talk, I'll share some details of our approach, lessons we learned, and ideas on how to scale this type of learning within an organization; I will also debut a publicly-accessible version of the course.
track_title: Being an informed and savvy AI user

title: High Quality R/Shiny Apps at Scale: Lessons from DaVinci’s Modular Framework
abstract: Scaling R/Shiny apps is hard: code gets duplicated, UX becomes inconsistent, and validation is expensive. With DaVinci, a Shiny framework for exploring clinical trial data, we address these issues through a modular approach. DaVinci provides reusable, qualified modules that follow shared standards for structure, interfaces, testing, and performance. This talk shows why modularity works at scale, how it speeds up delivery and improves quality, and how module developers, app creators, and app users work together to build robust apps. Attendees will learn practical patterns to improve consistency, maintainability, and validation effort – applicable to any team building many Shiny apps, not only in pharma.

title: From chats to workflows to “agents”: Demystifying LLM jargon by example
abstract:
If the phrase "agentic AI" has ever made you scratch your head (or roll your eyes), this talk is for you. The AI field is awash in jargon that sounds precise but isn't—and when every technology is branded as an "agent" or "agentic," it’s pretty hard to know what anyone is talking about. So, let's fix that. 

In this gentle, no-experience-required introduction to LLM systems, I'll demystify the jargon by building up from first principles. Using a single running example—turning messy clinical notes into a structured summary—we'll walk through four levels of LLM system design: chats, workflows, agents, and multi-agent systems. You'll leave with a better understanding of agentic design patterns and how to try them out for yourself.
track_title: Being an informed and savvy AI user

title: Better Notebooks with Marimo: Reproducible Data Science Workflows
abstract:
Interactive notebooks are foundational in applied data science, but they introduce their own problems: out-of-order execution, difficult storage formats, and input-output mixing. Marimo is a modern Python notebook system that tackles these problems head-on. Reactive execution ensures reproducibility, its script-based format works well with version control and a broader Python codebase, and its outputs stay separate from inputs.

But Marimo offers even more. This talk will show how Marimo notebooks fit naturally into analytics projects, focusing both on code features—pytest compatibility and its Python script format—and editor features, including a VS Code extension, LLM support, and Quarto integration.

title: Notebooks and Beyond: Mapping the Data Science Interface Spectrum
abstract: Data science rarely happens in a single tool anymore. Between the terminal, IDEs, notebooks, and now AI-driven interfaces, the question isn't which tool wins, but where each one actually fits. This talk aims to map that spectrum: the speed of the command line, the structure of IDEs like Positron, reactive notebooks like Marimo, and the newer prompt-driven canvas spaces. Along the way, I'll look at how these environments complement each other in practice, where AI tools genuinely help versus where they just add noise, and why reproducible code needs to stay the source of truth no matter which interface you're working in.

title: Positron and the Three Bears: Teaching Python with Positron
abstract:
For polyglot data science, RStudio is too specific, VS Code is too general, but Positron is just right. However, it’s not without friction. With two years of experience teaching Python with Positron, I’ll discuss how Positron fits in the data stack and how it helps address the “three bears” of teaching Python:

1. Installing Python and managing virtual environments
2. Creating GitHub-friendly notebook workflows
3. Accessing scalable compute resources

I hope my experience with Positron can help other attendees in their professional and personal efforts as instructors and mentors.

title: Delivering Automations at Scale: {rtemplate} for High‑Throughput Biomarker Analytics
abstract: Supporting hundreds of biomarker focused clinical and exploratory studies requires fast, standardized, and reproducible early stage analyses in the biopharma industry. After exploring approaches and needs of analysts and scientists, our team converged on {rtemplate} - an R based automation framework that easily delivers structured data via {arrow}, an orchestrated analysis pipeline via {targets}, consistent figure standards via {ggplot2}, and Quarto powered {shiny} viewers. With by AI assisted feature development, {rtemplate} enables teams to meet tight timelines while shifting analyst time toward the deep, high impact scientific work that matches the reality of clinical and exploratory biomarker workloads. Developed in collaboration with Peter Ehmann, previously with Regeneron, now with Merck & Co., Inc.

title: Making the Impossible Possible: A Software-First Stack for Resource-Constrained Research
abstract: At Drexel's Urban Health Collaborative, we study how climate change affects health across US and Latin American cities — complex work run by a small team with no enterprise budget. I'll share how Posit's code-first products took us from ad hoc data management to a software-first organization. Starting from RStudio, Quarto turned pipelines into reproducible notebooks and Positron opened the door to Python tools like dbt-DuckDB. That let us adopt analytics engineering, GitHub-driven development, and Notion for non-technical collaboration — shipping model-ready data fast. This code-first stack is ready for what's next: agentic AI. Attendees leave with a playbook for a lightweight data stack resource-constrained teams can adopt incrementally.

title: From Programming Alone to Programming and Prompting: Teaching Bilingual AI-Enabled Data Science with Positron and Quarto
abstract: Most courses teach R or Python. I teach both—in the same Quarto documents, using Positron. Students start with parallel tracks (bag-of-words, NLP in both languages), then shift mid-semester to integrated workflows: R for preprocessing, Python for transformers. But I've moved beyond programming alone. Prompt engineering starts week two. GitHub Copilot and Positron Assistant are available from day one, with prompting exercises in every lab. These bilingual, AI-augmented skills are essential. One surprise: students with no prior programming experience end up more bilingual than those who arrive knowing one language. No home base to retreat to. I'll share what's working, what's not, and how Positron and Quarto make this practical.

title: Designing Reproducible Learning Ecosystems with R and Quarto
abstract: Reproducibility in data science is often taught as a final requirement rather than as a workflow that evolves over time. This talk presents a reproducible learning ecosystem built with R and Quarto that moves learners from one-off assignments to durable, public work—and ultimately into contributors. Learners iteratively refactor their analyses into portfolio books, contribute to a shared research volume built on real civic data, and engage with open tooling that lowers barriers to authentic analysis. The session focuses on design decisions, lessons learned, and practical patterns for teaching reproducibility through iteration, ownership, and real-world data.

title: Bridging the Gap: Custom Catalogs to Connect End Users with Data Products
abstract: For data scientists today, creating stellar apps and reports is not enough without proper dissemination to the end users. Our team has created dozens of Shiny apps and Quarto reports which can be useful to the wider organization. Now, to bridge the gap between our users and data products, we have developed an interactive catalog with Quarto Dashboard, the connectapi R package, and a content tags hierarchy on Connect. We aim to help end-users explore our offerings and quickly find the tools they can most benefit from. My talk will demonstrate how any data analytics team can easily build their own custom catalog to better communicate with their end users.

title: The Tableau Plateau: From Dashboards to AI-Ready Data Products
abstract: At Suffolk, we hit a “Tableau plateau.” Our team had split into two tribes: point-and-click dashboard builders and code-first data scientists. BI tools felt faster - but capped our technical ceiling. By standardizing on Shiny, using Git-backed deployment for Posit Connect, and leveraging AI coding agents like Positron Assistant, we flipped the equation. With Shiny modules and brand.yml providing guardrails for developers and agents, we standardized structure, styling, and patterns. Code not only surpassed point-and-click tools in speed - it produced extensible products built for ML and AI integration. This shift unified our team and transformed dashboards from reporting artifacts into AI-ready data products.

title: Everything you wanted to know about agents* (*but were afraid to ask)
abstract:
Agents, agents, agents. The practice of software development has been transformed by AI coding agents like Claude Code. The practice data science is also being changed by AI coding agents, but not quite in the same way. Data science uses many of the same tools and techniques as pure software development, but at its heart there is a fundamental difference: with software development, the goal is to build something, but with data analysis, the goal is to learn something.

With that in mind, I’ll talk about:
- What is an agent?
- How do they work?
- What are they good at, and what are they bad at?
- How is software development different from data science?
- How can you maximize your trust in agent’s work?

title: Great Docs: Beautiful Documentation Sites for Python Packages
abstract:
Documentation is one of the most impactful things you can do for your Python package (and one of the most tedious to set up). Between manually cataloging your API, wrestling with configuration, and keeping everything in sync as your code evolves, many projects ship with incomplete docs (or none).

Great Docs eliminates this friction. A single command auto-discovers your package's public API and generates a complete, professionally styled documentation site. It also auto-generates llms.txt files, creates license and citation pages, and gives you a polished landing page, organized API reference, and User Guide section.

In this talk, I'll introduce Great Docs, walk through its workflow, and demo sites I've built for several Python projects.

title: Less to decide, more to reuse: the block in blockr
abstract: We present blockr, a framework for interactively building data workflows, developed in collaboration with Bristol-Myers Squibb. Implemented as a modular set of R packages, blockr suits applications from interactive dashboards to static reports. The break-down into well-defined steps, along with AI assistance, provides a natural, no-code interface to complex problems. A block is a deliberately restricted unit of computation, and this is what lets the same blocks be reused across very different applications. We show what it takes to write a block. We then look at a production app built almost entirely from general-purpose blocks, with domain-specific ones only where the problem demands them, and an AI assistant to assemble them.

title: Debugging Is a Nightmare: Meaningful Metaphors for Data Science Education
abstract: Metaphor and analogy are often treated as rhetorical flourishes, but they play a real role in how we learn technical concepts. In data science education, metaphors help make invisible processes visible and support transfer from familiar experience into abstract reasoning. This talk treats “debugging is a nightmare” as more than a phrase, using it to guide concrete practices like “dream journaling” (minimal reproducible examples), “lucid dreaming” (stepping through code), and “magic apples” (capturing state). It then steps back to reflect on how such frames shape learners’ reasoning, where they help, where they break down, and what educators should be deliberate about in choosing appropriate metaphors.

title: Finding Common Language between Data Scientists and Non Data Scientists
abstract: Data scientists need to communicate effectively with stakeholders who do not have a programming background but do have detailed technical knowledge in an area where the data scientist is not an expert. Finding the right shared language helps minimize wasted work, especially early in a project. For example: cooking recipes can serve as an analogous data set understood by synthesis chemists and data scientists working on chemical reaction data. Use of a common language reduces the amount of brainpower spent interpreting terminology and allows everyone to focus on design goals – data visualizations, search interfaces, data sources, etc. This talk will provide advice for finding a shared language topic and examples of how they can be used.

title: SELECT instance FROM cloud WHERE workload = ? ORDER BY cost_efficiency
abstract:
Selecting the right cloud instance for DS/ML/AI workloads is still mostly guesswork. Pricing and hardware specs exist, but fragmented across providers and hard to compare, especially when real workload performance matters.

We introduce Spare Cores Navigator, an open dataset covering thousands of cloud instance types across vendors with standardized performance and cost-efficiency metrics. We show how instance choice becomes a simple data task in R or Python: filter by workload, hardware, compliance, or budget, then rank candidates by price-performance to identify the most efficient option for your workload.

title: Finding Care Fast: An R Shiny App for Infectious Disease Exposure Response
abstract: Local public health agencies must rapidly coordinate testing and vaccination for people who have been exposed to infectious diseases. At DeKalb Public Health, epidemiologists previously relied on manual Google Maps searches to identify the closest of four health centers for each patient. To address this complicated and time-consuming process, I developed an R Shiny app that ranks centers by driving distance using ZIP code centroids to preserve privacy. I utilized the openrouteserve API to calculate the distances and used the leaflet package to create interactive maps. The app supports single and batch address workflows, reduces coordination time, and demonstrates how open-source tools can have real-world impact in public health.

title: Keynote Sessions: Correct, reproducible, and transparent data agents (Sara & Simon), Building the Future of Data Science and AI with Posit and AWS (Jagjit Dhaliwal)
abstract:
9 - 9:55am | How do we build competent data analysis agents? Data analysis requires a willingness to pause, question conclusions, dig into subtleties, and sit with uncertainty. Frontier LLMs, however, are optimized to push tasks toward completion rather than refraining from answering unanswerable questions. Drawing on our experience building data analysis agents, we'll share evaluations that expose where LLM-driven analysis goes wrong and design patterns that keep analyses correct, transparent, and reproducible.

9:55 - 10:05am | Building the Future of Data Science and AI with Posit and AWS

title: Positron for Everyone: Organization-Wide Posit Tooling on Amazon SageMaker
abstract: Unlock the full potential of your analytics team by deploying Positron as a managed, organization-wide environment within Amazon SageMaker Studio. This joint session with Posit and AWS explores how to provide analysts with a browser-based, scalable IDE equipped with R, Python, and Quarto, all while maintaining seamless AWS integration. We will detail the analyst experience, including built-in AI assistance via Bedrock-powered Posit Assistant, and provide technical insights for platform teams on managing deployments, licensing, and security at scale. Eliminate local environment friction and empower your organization with a unified, cloud-native workspace.

title: Do This Instead: 5 Powerful and Empowering Alternatives to Common Charts
abstract:
Even in “good” charts, it’s easy to miss or misinterpret key patterns in the data. Common best practices — continuous color scales, equally spaced gridlines, month-level aggregation, etc — leave critical leaps from numbers to meaning up to visual perception and unexamined assumptions.

“Do This Instead” offers 5 specific before/after replacements for common analysis situations. For example, grouping continuous values into meaningful categories lets us use facet_wrap to create small multiples instead of relying on color perception. And, explicitly defining what counts as “high” creates a shared, expertise-grounded interpretation. 

Techniques are tool-agnostic; examples implemented in ggplot.​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​

title: Quack to the Future: Building Traceable Data Lakehouses with DuckLake in R
abstract: Modern data pipelines need more than clean outputs: they need a paper trail. This talk introduces two R packages to help you build a lakehouse stack using DuckLake for transactional storage and dplyneage for column-level lineage tracking. We'll walk through a medallion architecture (bronze → silver → gold) built with dplyr familiar workflows, where every table write is versioned with author and commit message. You'll see how to visualize lineage flows across pipeline layers, time-travel back to earlier table versions, and audit exactly how your data changed and why, all without leaving R.

title: Building a Custom Version of GeoGuessr in R
abstract: This is about using R creatively for non-traditional tasks, with an example of building a custom version of the game GeoGuessr in R. Attendees at this session will learn not only about the tools to build this, but how to innovatively solve problems in R. The process starts by taking a non-technical idea: a version of GeoGuessr just for New York City. Then breaking it down into smaller parts that R can handle: developing a Shiny dashboard frontend for players to interact with, encoding gameplay into data structures in Google Sheets for easy access for players, and building a backend to collect and process data from APIs. Attendees can play the live game with locations from the host city, Houston, to see R powering real-time gameplay.

title: ORCA: a collaboratively-built AI-powered Shiny app built on Posit Team
abstract: ORCA is KS&R’s internal Shiny application for AI-assisted coding of open-ended survey responses. Designed in concert with Ketchbrook Analytics, ORCA combines an intuitive front-end for job submission, response review, and code editing with a modular backend built on the Posit ecosystem. The system integrates a {golem}-based Shiny app, a plumber API for asynchronous processing, pins for versioned metadata, and scheduled batch workflows for logging and delivery. This talk showcases how thoughtful UI/UX design and Posit-based infrastructure work together to operationalize AI in a transparent, reproducible research environment.

title: Reusing 'ggplot2' code: how to design better plot helper functions
abstract: Creating 'ggplot2' helper functions can help avoid repeatedly copying and pasting long and complex 'ggplot2' code chunks. However, if helper functions are not carefully designed, the initial convenience can often turn into frustration. While helper functions can reduce the amount of code needed to remake a complicated plot, they often mask the underlying layered grammar of graphics, complicating further customisation and tweaking of the plot. This talk addresses how to design effective 'ggplot2' plot helper functions that maximise reuse convenience whilst preserving access to the elegant flexibility of layered plot composition.

title: From Dplyr to Polars: Migrating Tools & Languages While Maintaining the Tidy Model
abstract: Many data practitioners who learned analysis through R’s dplyr, discover that moving to Python can feel like losing a native language. I certainly felt that way, and my colleagues tend to echo the same sentiments. Learning new syntax is easy, but porting the mental model the tidyverse provides was the real challenge. In this talk I describe my personal migration from dplyr to Polars and how I rebuilt the mental model in a new ecosystem. I draw on my personal opinions and experience, the thoughts of colleagues, and the objective differences in technical goals and specifications. The goal of this talk is to show data practitioners how to preserve the workflows they loved in dplyr with the execution model of polars in python.
track_title: The Evolving Craft of Data Science

title: From internal scripts to public portfolios: building an open source program at Dow
abstract: Dow's Citizen Data Science community is putting R and Python into the hands of chemical researchers across the company. As these data science workflows matured, we saw an opportunity: share our general-purpose tools with the broader community through an open source release program. This talk walks through how we built that program -- the policy, the legal review process, the release checklist -- and piloted it with six R packages for statistical analysis and experimental design. Attendees will leave with a practical playbook for standing up an open source release program at organizations where one doesn't yet exist.

title: Life after R4DS: How to take your R skills to the next level
abstract:
Picture this: You've taken that difficult first step into learning R, and you've worked your way through a course, workshop, or online textbook like "R for Data Science". Your foundation is solid - but now what?

This talk will give you the resources you need to take your R skills to the next level. First, I will discuss the three ABCs of pathways forward to Intermediate R: Analysis of complex data, Building professional deliverables, and Coding/programming.

Then, I will share a new public course site designed for both classroom use and for self-guided learners. The course takes a "learn by doing" approach, with modular tracks structured around project that is completed progressively through hands-on exercises.

title: Cairn: From notebooks to logbooks
abstract: Notebooks let you rewrite history. Logbooks don't. In logbook-mode analysis, history is a first-class citizen: cells, commentary, and AI exchanges are only ever appended so that the document becomes a chronological record of every step performed in a data analysis. I'll show why notebook software doesn't fully accommodate this style, and introduce Cairn, my attempt at supporting it properly: a Neovim plugin for stacking your analysis one stone at a time.
track_title: The Evolving Craft of Data Science

title: Positron Everywhere All At Once
abstract:
A modern data science IDE has to feel the same wherever someone opens it. Data scientists move constantly between personal laptops, shared servers, containerized workflows, and the mix of cloud and on-prem environments that shape day-to-day work. The tools they rely on need to travel with them.

Positron, a next-generation data science IDE, is one of those tools. Deploying it means meeting people on the platforms they already use. In this talk, I'll share strategies for bringing Positron to academic settings, where instructors and students juggle personal machines, course JupyterHub deployments, and department servers. I'll walk through real examples of running Positron Server through JupyterHub via jupyter-server-proxy, configuring it for classroom use, and weighing the tradeoffs of each approach. You'll leave with practical techniques for common academic deployment scenarios and a clearer sense of where Positron fits today.
track_title: The Evolving Craft of Data Science

title: From ABC to AI: Applying Language Acquisition to R and Technical Mastery
abstract:
The world’s most spoken language isn’t Python. It is English. As a second language learner who struggled before later teaching English and authoring a book on R, I learned that fluency comes from internalizing structure. 

In the age of AI, if models can generate code instantly, does learning R still matter? 

This talk introduces a Three Layer Model of Technical Mastery: 

Syntax, the vocabulary that AI accelerates; 
Structure, the grammar of tidyverse, Quarto, and Shiny workflows; 
Thinking, the human skills of framing problems and making judgments.

By mapping language learning to the evolution of a data scientist, this talk offers a practical framework for building durable skills in an AI assisted world.

title: How Shiny changed data analysis at the Metabolism Center
abstract: Scientists in metabolic research increasingly rely on technologies measuring thousands of targets simultaneously, but many are still limited to analyses in spreadsheets Introducing Shiny transformed how our center works with data: an ecosystem of apps now gives researchers tools that once required coding, enabling faster exploration and richer insights. Data can be easily visualized with datasets from other researchers, allowing analysis in a broader context. Junior researchers are building new apps, sharing their analysis pipelines with the world. I will share some of our success stories, and highlight the packages we use to make apps fast, interactive, and intuitive.

title: Quarto Hub: Collaboratively edit, create, and share documents
abstract: Quarto Hub is a new open-source and hosted platform from Posit. In Quarto Hub, you can create, edit, comment on, and publish your Quarto projects (single documents, presentations, websites) collaboratively. In this talk, we will give an overview of how it works, and how Quarto Hub interacts with existing code-first practices and text-based workflows. We will show how the architecture of Quarto Hub allows a variety of use cases, including (if time permits) integration with RStudio, Positron, and Posit AI.

title: From, "Can you Just Make Us a Dashboard" to Enterprise Systems in R
abstract: Over the past five years, Mayo Clinic’s Data Visualization Lab has grown from three statisticians building simple dashboards in R into an enterprise team delivering production Shiny systems that support real clinical and operational decision-making. This talk shares lessons learned from scaling open-source tools in a highly regulated healthcare environment, where data are siloed, workflows are complex, and trust matters. I’ll discuss how we moved from ad-hoc dashboards to governed, maintainable applications using R, Shiny, REDCap, and Posit Connect, and what it took organizationally to make the shift succeed. Attendees will leave with concrete patterns for building credibility and responsibly scaling R-based systems in high-stakes settings.

title: Instant Feedback, Robust Evals: Agentic AI Tutoring in R and Python
abstract: What if every open source data science resource included practice coding problems with immediate feedback? I made blendtutor and blendtutor-py so educators can hand-craft coding lessons installed as an R package or Python module. Learners then get immediate agentic AI-powered feedback on their code. And we don’t have to just hope the LLMs provide useful pointers. These packages give scaffolding to create custom LLM evals for every lesson. No matter the learning goal, educators can create lessons where LLMs steer learners in a helpful direction. The best version of these packages involves co-evolution with the community. I’m excited to figure out together how this active learning can support other open source resources.

title: The Design of Everyday R Functions
abstract:
You might think "design" only applies to physical objects or visual interfaces like Shiny apps. But as Don Norman noted in The Design of Everyday Things, "all artificial things are designed." If users struggle with your code, it's a design flaw, not human error. Fortunately, good design isn't just for designers.

In this talk, I'll show you how to make your R functions easier to use. You'll learn how to better signify what a function does, how to be forgiving when users are a bit sloppy, and how to clearly explain what to do when your code can't fix a problem for them. I'll also equip you to teach AI agents to follow these principles, making your R functions easier to use even if you're the only user.

title: When the data doesn’t fit the question
abstract: As the largest public funder of biomedical research worldwide, the National Institutes of Health has a responsibility to track the impact of its funding. An important metric for impact is research publications; however, publication databases are used across the scientific community without consideration of their integrity. These publication databases were often created prior to the development of fair data practices; therefore assessment of their current data integrity is critical. I assessed the data integrity of these databases using R and the tidyverse. I developed techniques for defining limitations, identifying standards, and refining analysis to ensure these databases are reviewed with integrity and used to their fullest potential.

title: Environmental Stressors and Healthcare: How a Posit/R Powered Pipeline Reveals Environmental Drivers of Emergency Department Strain
abstract: Extreme heat and poor air quality strain Emergency Department (ED) operations. We scaled a Baytown pilot across Houston Methodist (HM) and packaged it for Texas Medical Center (TMC) partners using an end-to-end Posit stack. We integrate Epic/Clarity with EPA Air Quality System and NOAA Climate Data Online, model ED counts with tidymodels, and build spatial visualizations of ED demand across the HM service area with environmental hazard/amenity overlays (refineries, green space). We deliver Quarto reports for managers and a Shiny dashboard for leaders. Protected Health Information stays in database; artifacts are versioned (pins), served (vetiver), orchestrated (targets), and hosted on-network. A template repo enables sharing across TMC.

title: Lowering Cesarean Rates  - Using Quarto to Create Scalable Performance Reports
abstract: Cesarean births can be lifesaving, but overuse carries health risks and financial costs. At the Obstetrics Initiative, we partner with 65+ Michigan hospitals to reduce unnecessary cesareans and improve maternal care. As Analytics Manager, I lead the development of performance reports built on near real-time EHR data to monitor trends, identify opportunities, and guide targeted support. We rely on Quarto to power scalable reporting pipelines and custom, one-off analyses. In this talk, I’ll share practical tips for using Quarto to build impactful analytics tools your stakeholders will actually use—and value.

title: Operationalizing Quality: Building an ICU Dashboard at the VA with Shiny
abstract:
In the high-stakes environment of the VA Critical Care Service Line, data silos often hinder rapid decision-making. We replaced static, retrospective reporting with a production-grade Shiny dashboard to track key quality metrics across the VA Pittsburgh Healthcare System.

This talk explores the journey of building an operational tool that connects directly to the VA Corporate Data Warehouse (CDW). I will demonstrate how we leverage R and SQL to visualize complex clinical data, democratize access for leadership, and navigate the unique security constraints of a federal IT environment. Attendees will learn strategies for moving from "metrics on a spreadsheet" to interactive, reproducible dashboards that drive real clinical change.

title: Flipping the Switch
abstract: Open source adoption is widely discussed, yet few enterprises complete a full digital transformation using only open source tools and languages. GSK R&D flipped the switch, moving 3,000+ colleagues from proprietary stacks to an open source. This session explains how we built a leadership-ready cost, risk, and productivity model; secured executive sponsorship; and planned the migration in waves without disrupting research delivery. We will cover governance, training, internal champions, and metrics that kept teams productive, plus what we would do differently. Attendees will learn how to take small organizations and experiments to full enterprise digital transformation so they can make the case to their own leaders.

title: CancerTrialsBR: Improving Access to Cancer Clinical Trials in Brazil with R, Shiny and Large Language Models
abstract: A lack of timely, accessible information is a major barrier to cancer trial recruitment. We present CancerTrialsBR, a Shiny app. that combines R, Google Maps, and LLM to improve access to trial information in Brazil. A daily R pipeline retrieves data from ClinicalTrials.gov, uses LLM to generate Portuguese summaries and descriptors, and standardize facilities with Google Maps. This enriched database can be accessed through a Shiny app., and users interact to suggest status alterations which are validated before integration. This project has partnered with the Brazilian Society of Clinical Oncology since Nov. 2025 and had 4,030 visits from 220 Brazilian cities. User feedback resulted in 34/57 updated status incorporated in the database.

title: Open Source Routing Analysis at Scale
abstract: Routing analysis is critical for understanding access to government services. My colleagues and I researched how access to Social Security Administration offices might change if some offices were to close, which the federal government proposed last year. However, nationwide routing analysis presents challenges: Google Maps API is prohibitively expensive, and open source OSRM's online server is for demonstration only. In this talk, we'll share how we used R, bash, and Docker to deploy a local OSRM server for nationwide routing analysis, present our findings on office closures, and explain how we're leveraging this infrastructure to enable future research on service accessibility.

title: Quarto + Accessibility + You
abstract:
New accessibility requirements from your organization might feel like a barrier between you and the tools you rely on. The irony? Accessibility is about removing barriers between your work and the people who need it. Fortunately, the landscape for Quarto users is rapidly improving.

In this talk, I'll share what's new in Quarto and related tools that make producing accessible documents easier than ever. You'll learn what you need to know as a Quarto user to ensure your work reaches everyone who needs it.

title: Can I offer you a nice IDE in this trying time?
abstract: Adopting new tools means overcoming a learning curve, motivated by familiarity with added benefits or by new and worthwhile capabilities. This happens with IDE use in research and education, where RStudio can be synonymous with R itself. Since Positron's release as a multilingual data science IDE, experienced users quickly saw its potential, but many others remained hesitant. Missing RStudio features caused resistance, while capabilities like multiple R installations, fast exploration of large datasets, and spreadsheet extensions drove wider adoption. This talk highlights how incremental, user-centered improvements can lower the barriers to entry. Switching IDEs depends not just on novel features, but on addressing unspoken frustrations.

title: Friends till the End(-to-end): Moving R and Python Projects into Pipelines with targets and Hamilton
abstract:
Using R and Python within the same project liberates data scientists to work with whoever and whatever (software) they want. But moving these projects from notebooks into production can feel like picking a favorite child: which language should control the pipeline? 

I want to empower polyglot data scientists to face this choice head-on by sharing my experience building mixed language pipelines with R's 'targets' package and Python's 'Hamilton' package. Because these packages share similar, "functional" syntax to define pipelines, data scientists can use the same logic in both languages! I demonstrate the pros and cons of each choice by showing how I moved a ‘targets’ pipeline into ‘Hamilton’ to solve collaborative and technical challenges.

title: Slideware Is Dead - Long Live Quarto
abstract:
There have been, over the years, many reasons why one would use PowerPoint, Canva, and Keynote over Quarto for making slides.

Despite many of the core features from quarto, such as code results and humanly readable file formats, there are still some tactile elements that 
makes slideware favourable to the code-focused Quarto slides.

This will go over the changes in Quarto itself and the slide-specific features that make the experience of creating slides in Quarto just as nice as in any other software.

This includes, but is not limited to: allowing you to move and center images, add arrows, and fix typos directly in the slides.

title: Clinical data harmonization with LLMs
abstract: Clinical trial data formats differ across studies and over time, even within an organization. After years of writing bespoke R code to harmonize data for cross-study analysis, my team is developing LLM-assisted automation. First, we use an LLM to develop a data model for the output, describing a format and content that accommodates all input studies. Then an LLM evaluates each study’s data files and documentation to determine how to wrangle each input file to fit the data model. The LLM generates yaml configuration files for programmatically transforming each study into an interoperable format for combined analysis. Our LLM prompts, data model, configuration files, and pipeline code are all version controlled and reproducible.

title: Running a software department in times of agents
abstract:
This abstract might be written by some LLM tool. The majority of the work we used to do is different right now. The challenges my team faces in February might be quite different in September.

I'm the Head of Technology at Appsilon, which means that I take care of around 40 R and Python devs across dozens of projects. My daily work is heavily affected by the AI revolution: I advise on the best tools, react to the expectations that "vibe-coding" will do the job, handle recruitment fraud attempts, and build complex-packages-specialized AI agents.

The audience will have the opportunity to hear my experiences on how AI works on scale, from the front-line perspective of a company for which leveraging AI properly is an existential challenge.
track_title: The Evolving Craft of Data Science

title: The NASA Earthdata Cloud Cookbook: A Quarto Collaboration Story
abstract: A shared problem can help unite people to work together for a common solution, which they can then adapt to address further needs. NASA Earthdata staff manage over 100 petabytes of data and create tutorials to help scientists access these data with code. Since 2021, Quarto has helped NASA Openscapes mentors solve a shared problem by being a place to unite and build tutorials together, creating a “Cookbook” of Python and R tutorials with less redundancy – and help establish open source practices across a government agency. We'll share how over 5 years of Cookbook collaboration and governance have shaped these mentors' workflows, letting them focus on what matters: helping scientists work with NASA Earthdata efficiently.

title: First Impressions Matter: Styling Data Products That People Actually Want to Use
abstract: Professional styling isn't a luxury for data products—it determines whether users engage with our insights or click away. But for data scientists already managing complex code, mastering CSS to achieve polished results can feel overwhelming. This talk demonstrates how Bootswatch and brand.yml help you create professionally styled HTML-based products without CSS expertise. You'll learn to leverage ready-made themes with pick-and-choose YAML-based customization, taking your data products from functional-but-forgettable to professional and memorable tools people trust and rely on. Whether building internal dashboards or public-facing applications, you'll leave with practical examples and techniques to implement immediately.

title: Never Block, Never Copy: mirai + mori from Shiny to the Cluster
abstract:
Most parallel R is batch-and-wait: send off your tasks, wait for the slowest — and you're locked out while it runs. In a Shiny app, every user freezes. There's a quieter cost: eight workers each need their own copy of your data, so a 200 MB data frame becomes 1.6 GB to serialize, move, and hold in RAM. Your laptop habits die at deployment.

This talk shows you how to fix both problems with two CRAN packages, mirai and mori, building a production-ready memory model for event-loop applications. mirai keeps the event loop moving: it processes results as they arrive instead of blocking, and it's first-class in Shiny. When many users show up at once,

mirai can put a hard cap on how much data waits in the queue. When that limit is reached, it hands back control to your app rather than freezing every session. mori, on the other hand, removes the pressure at source: put a dataset into shared memory once and every worker maps the same pages, so 200 MB per worker collapses to a 200-byte reference, with no changes to your downstream code.

The same app runs anywhere you have compute. A new HTTP launcher makes the cloud, Kubernetes, and Posit Workbench as easy to reach as your own servers over SSH or an HPC cluster through its scheduler, and moving between them takes a single line of configuration.

Scale further. Scale safely. Never block, never copy — from your Shiny app to your cluster.

title: Teach Once, Use Often: Building AI Skills for Data Analysis
abstract: AI tools are increasingly part of the modern analyst's workflow—but generic prompting only gets you so far. Skills are structured prompts that teach an AI how to operate within a specific analytical context. In this talk, I'll walk through what skills are and why they matter, how to build one from scratch, and where to find community skills across Posit and other repositories. Along the way, I'll argue that developing a skill isn't just about configuring an AI—it's a valuable exercise in clarifying your own priorities, best practices, and standards for success. Rather than removing the analyst from the process, it can put them front and center. This talk will focus on the analyst and how they can use these tools to improve their work.

title: LLM-Powered Data Workflows: Structuring Inputs and Accelerating Insight
abstract: As organizations scale, the bottleneck is rarely data availability — it’s operationalizing that data reliably. Automation demands structure, yet real-world inputs are inconsistent, and even clean datasets require time-consuming interpretation before decisions can be made. This session presents two production LLM-powered systems: one that semantically standardizes unpredictable raw datasets for downstream automation, and another that transforms structured survey data into executive-ready narratives and interactive insights. Together, they illustrate how LLMs can enable scalable, decision-ready data workflows across the lifecycle.

title: Package Your Judgment, Keep Your Intent
abstract: Judgment is the capacity; your creative process is its observable trace. Every conversation with your agent is exactly that — a trace. You're already sharing your expertise, every day, with an audience of one. The alternative: package your judgment, keep your intent. This talk shows what that means in practice. At the UN we packaged our methodological judgment as a portable kit: a Python package, an MCP server, and a skill set that turns a generic coding agent into an opinionated pair-analyst for self-service analytics. You'll leave with a simple framework for what to package and what to keep, a structural answer to 'won't this replace me?' (it doesn't), and two public-good reasons to share your judgment."

title: Principles for Effective Interactive Visualizations
abstract: Many interactive visualizations start from what libraries make easy like allowing hovering, brushing, and zooming rather than what analysis actually needs. The result is dashboards that look interactive but rarely change how people think about their data. This talk presents principles for designing meaningful interaction: how to identify which dimensions reward interactivity, how affordance design shapes user behavior, and how interactive composition can deepen exploration. We ground these ideas in live notebook examples and introduce vibewidget, an open-source Python library built on anywidget, that uses natural language to rapidly prototype interactive visualizations, making it practical to test and refine interaction ideas in real time.

title: Crying, Caching, and Compiling: The Five Stages of R Optimization
abstract:
Is slow code giving you grief? Try working through the five stages:
1. Denial: My code WORKS. My tests are PASSING. Fine, I’ll try profiling.
2. Anger: dplyr::mutate() is that slow?!
3. Bargaining (aka caching): If I just store more in memory, then I don’t have to deal with compute time.
4. Depression: R is an interpreted language. Sometimes those are just slow. emo::ji(“sad”)
5. Acceptance: I’ll rewrite one critical function in Rust. Hope I don’t have to edit it later.
This presentation will guide non-programmers through speeding up their R code ranging from simple programming principles to incorporating Rust. Using examples from optimizing our tidywater package, you’ll learn to make code faster without sacrificing readability (too much).

title: It Worked Great Until I Left
abstract:
Recently I completed a project that I was really proud of. It worked great, and stakeholders were happy. Then I went on paternity leave, and the process I had built proved to be too complex to be handed off: everything broke. The underlying data wouldn't populate and the report wouldn't run. It took me returning to work to get everything back up and running.

This is a cautionary tale of how I let complexity creep in, how defaulting to familiar tools made my system harder to maintain, and how stepping back allowed me to identify the right tool for the job and simplify things. It is a reminder to build for the future maintainer and to always listen to the voice in your head that says "there has to be an easier way to do this."

title: Prepare locally, run remotely: Easily scale Tidymodels on Databricks with sparklyr
abstract:
Historically, accelerating large grid searches meant moving to expensive grid computing or complex "do-it-yourself" Spark clusters. Even with the infrastructure, it usually required changing R code significantly to make it work. These barriers make it hard for a practitioner to justify the cost of money and effort in their daily work.

Today, Databricks has made high-performance Spark clusters easy to manage. In this session, we demonstrate how to off-load tuning jobs from a local R session to Databricks. Using the exact same Tidymodels objects, sparklyr automatically performs model evaluation in a parallel and distributed manner. Practitioners can now easily accelerate large grid searches at scale without refactoring.

title: How I Automated My Job, Cashed Out and Developed 6-Pack Abs Using AI!
abstract: It's hard to balance the skepticism that comes from the assault of social media-based AI hype with the fear of missing out and becoming obsolete. Am I falling behind? Can AI do all my coding better than I can? Who is this Lang and why do I keep hearing about their chain? We've all been in meetings where management wants to see ROI from AI investments, and we've all had to navigate vendors promising the world and coming up short. In this talk, I will give some actionable insights for navigating the fast-paced space, some pitfalls that I've experienced and how to extract true value from the perspective of an average data scientist at a pharmaceutical company just trying to level up his kid's college fund.

title: Roll for Wisdom: What AI Gets Wrong About Data Analysis
abstract:
AI tools have been excellent for writing software. We can turn an agent loose and feel relatively confident that we can achieve a good result since we can verify changes via unit tests. 

However, it often falls flat for some types of data analysis. I think the reason is a lack of understanding of what a bad idea is and other aspects of common sense. The situation is similar to D&D's conceptions of intelligence versus wisdom: raw facts versus reason. 

I'll give some examples of: poor data analysis choices, information leakage, and overfitting to its training set.

title: Fake it Til' You Make It: Mocking Reality So Your Tests Can Run
abstract:
As data scientists mature in their work, many move from analysis scripts to larger codebases and packages, bringing unit testing into the workflow. For some, a handful of basic tests is enough. For others, as code grows more complex, familiar testing patterns may start to break.

We’ll explore testing in isolation as a practical way to handle more challenging programming scenarios. We’ll cover the core ideas behind mocking and controlling your code’s environment while focusing on when, where, how, and why these techniques help in real projects. The talk is intended for anyone already comfortable with unit testing who wants to explore strategies for isolating behavior, reducing test fragility, and expanding test coverage for complex systems.

title: Keynote Session: Navigating the Agentic Future
abstract: Agents are taking over a growing share of day to day coding work. As models and harnesses continue to improve, where are we still needed? What skills must we develop to be effective and successful in this agent-powered future? In this talk I'll share my perspective after more than a year of using agents to create many large new codebases for software engineering and data work. I'll make the case that the things that have always mattered—human agency, good taste, and architectural thinking—are still what will determine whether we succeed or fail.

title: Three Agents, Two Mistakes, or Designing for LLM-Assisted Data Analysis
abstract:
We've built three data science agents at Posit over the last eighteen months, each one a correction of the last. Positron Assistant was focused just on writing code itself, and so was too rigid to keep up with the iterative work of data science. Databot lacked the depth needed for start-to-finish workflows because it was an expert in one thing, exploratory data analysis. Posit Assistant is what we built once we understood what we needed both: a fast, flexible coding agent that is also an expert in data science.

This talk is about the design decisions in between each iteration, and why the harness around a model matters more than the model inside it. Each mistake taught us part of why: every data science feature we added to a generic coding agent made that agent harder to change, and an agent's autonomy is only as good as what it has access to.

The demos are in Positron; the principles aren't.

title: Between Code and Conclusions: An Evaluation Layer for LLM-Generated Analysis
abstract: LLMs quickly analyze data, but they routinely violate statistical assumptions, ignore missing data patterns, and misinterpret what variables actually measure. In this talk, I'll show how Circuit, an evaluation layer for LLM-generated data analysis, catches these mistakes before they reach users. We built an API and semantic layer that sits between code execution and output, using R as a first-class language to detect both statistical errors (assumption violations, selection bias, ignored uncertainty) and ontological errors (misunderstanding what data means). You'll see real examples of failures Circuit prevents, learn how the architecture works, and leave with patterns for building guardrails into your own AI-assisted workflows.

title: Staying Organized Across Machines: Practical Workflows for Data Scientists with Busy Brains
abstract: Data science work can be chaotic even on a good day — and when you’re juggling multiple clients, multiple machines, and an ADHD brain, organization becomes mission‑critical. In this talk, I’ll share a cognitive‑friendly workflow built around Obsidian, Git, and reproducible R and Python projects that helps me stay focused and consistent across contexts. I’ll walk through how I manage cross‑machine notes, secure client information, integrate Obsidian tasks with Outlook calendars, and use Templater and backlinks to keep fast, messy notes connected to long‑term structure.Attendees will leave with lightweight, copy‑ready templates and habits they can use to stay organized — even when balancing complex projects, clients, and busy brains.

title: Building Confidence, Not Bugs: Internal Packages for Empowered Data Teams
abstract:
This talk details how I moved the team's core business logic from scattered scripts into a robust, version-controlled internal package to prevent recurrence. I will cover the transition from copy-paste to package maintenance and testing, and the importance of demystifying tool-building for non-engineers.
I will cover:
- Identifying when code needs a function, and when a function needs a package.
- Strategies for consistently hard-coding domain knowledge (e.g., categorizations, identifiers, offsets).
- Reduced onboarding time and increased confidence for junior team members—a major cultural win.
You will receive a roadmap for building their first internal package and the confidence to treat analysis code as the software product it is.

title: When English Is Second, R Comes First
abstract: English is my second language, and for years that meant hesitation in professional settings. I often had strong ideas but not always the words. In R, I found fluency. Through tools like ggplot2, Shiny, and Quarto, I discovered a language of precision where data visualization and interactive workflows communicate ideas clearly. This talk explores how the R ecosystem becomes more than a toolkit — it becomes a platform for confidence, community, and expression, showing how code can serve as a powerful medium for communication, not just computation.

title: Creating Ergonomic Informatics Solutions to Enhance Patient Care in the Digital Health Era
abstract: In the current digital health era, the need for rapid insights is nearing the expectation of real-time delivery. We present our experience developing on-demand data science pipelines atop the electronic medical record. Specifically, the topics of our use case examples focus on: 1) the utilization of continuous health monitoring data extracted from wearable devices in the inpatient setting, as well as, 2) the analytical environments leveraged to process high-volume signal measurements (e.g., sleep-wake patterns, actigraphy, sensory exposures). In alignment with learning health systems (LHS) models, our work demonstrates how informatics-driven insights can be harnessed to implement patient-centered workflow changes directly at the bedside.

title: Keynote Session: Context is the Control Plane
abstract: Context has always been critical to applied data work – long before artificial intelligence made it a buzzword. But why aren’t we nearly as intentional when curating context for ourselves as for agents? This talk will explore the many types of context data scientists require to do meaningful work – from the unarticulated questions motivating our work, the mechanics of the source systems responsible for delivering our data, the assumptions baked into every one of our tools, the tacit knowledge hidden from view in parallel disciplines, and the way we share our findings. Along the way, we will discuss practical tips for building and curating the context needed for data work and how this process is part of what keeps our field fundamentally creative and human.
